author: hoeschec
text:
althoufx- thanks for the reply and charts.

I have been trying to figure this one out for a couple days now...I am still inexperienced when it comes to trading, and I have a hard time deciphering the intricacies of finding engulfs vs. fake-outs on multiple time frames. The time frames are fractal, so it seems to me there is always an engulf/fake-out that could suggest the opposite of how I am viewing a particular trade opportunity.

The more I look, the more I see. The more I see the harder it is to keep it all straight in my mind.

Here is an example of how I would analyze this chart in real time (I am referring to your M1 chart and drew colored circles over the areas of interest for clarity).

Yes, there is seemingly an engulf at the blue circle (as you have pointed out). Bu the only reason we see that as an engulf is because it broke the high of the FL in the orange circle. In order for an engulf to be valid, price must engulf an original FL or FTR - not simply a FL/FTR that forms as a result of a reaction to a different FL or FTR further to the left. So technically, we would have to look left to determine if the engulf was legitimate.

Also, price action can form what appears to be an engulf when price is really only bouncing off a S/R flip level. This is where it gets tricky and I get confused...How could we have known the price spike shown in the black circle was a F/O and not a valid engulf to the downside? In retrospect we can decipher that it was indeed a F/O, but I'm not seeing a way to know that during the live formation of price action.

The complication gets even worse when I start reviewing different time frames- it is really hard to know where to start looking since price continues to bounce and react to previous historic levels. I suppose we would have to look left and see why price engulfed to the upside in the red circle to find out if the break of that high ended in a critical location where orders were remaining. I think the engulf tends to take place in areas of low significance, whereas fake outs are essentially the IT's searching for LQ by triggering stops and finding pockets where orders reside.

Sorry if this is hard to follow, I'm not good at describing this using words.

Thanks for your help and contribution!

author: Ataraxia
text:
Hoeschec

It looks like that is the last candle of the week before the market closes? There is basically no liquidity so spreads will widen. It is very common on all charting platforms that I've looked at to have an odd looking candle at the end of the week. It's just the market closing. What you are actually seeing is not really happening e.g. it's not a price move. Often if you look at where the price reopens at the beginning of a new week, it's pretty close to where the price was BEFORE the odd looking candle appeared (unless there is a significant weekend gap).
